title: How Often Should You Clean a Pool in Bali?
meta: Learn how often to clean your villa pool in Sanur, Bali. Practical tips on sun exposure, leaf fall, swimmer load, and a realistic weekly schedule.
intro: In Sanur, most villa pools need a proper clean every two to three days during dry season and daily through the rainy months. The exact rhythm depends on what grows over your waterline, how many people actually get in, and whether you fill with PDAM mains or a well. Below is a practical breakdown so you stop guessing and keep that water clear without wasting time or chemicals.

paragraphs: The short answer: it varies. A pool under open sky collects organic matter faster than one tucked behind a wall. In Sanur's warm, humid air, algae spores land on the surface within hours if the chemistry drifts even slightly out of range.

Your water source matters too. PDAM tap water carries a small chlorine residual, giving you a slight head start. Well water, common in older villas along Jalan Raya and the smaller lanes, can be harder or softer depending on where the borehole sits, and may introduce iron or calcium that stains tiles and clogs filters more quickly.

sections.h2: Sun, Salt Air, and the Trees Overhead
paragraphs: Bali sun is relentless from October through May. UV breaks down free chlorine fast, so a pool balanced at 7 am can be under-chlorinated by mid-afternoon. If your villa has coconut palms, frangipani, or banyan trees lining the street, expect husks, petals, and fine leaf litter to land in the water every single day.

Add the sea breeze rolling off the beach and you get a thin film of salt and organic particles on the surface. It looks harmless, but over a week it feeds surface algae and makes the water feel film-y when you swim.
bullets: Skim the surface at least once a day; twice if trees sit directly overhead.
Backwash or rinse the filter laterals weekly during peak leaf season (roughly November to March).
Wipe the tile line with a soft brush every few days to stop biofilm where salt dries.

sections.h2: How Many People Are Actually Swimming?
paragraphs: One adult taking an evening dip introduces far less oil, sunscreen, and sweat than a family of four plus two kids splashing for an hour. Every swimmer adds body oils, lotions, and skin cells that the filter must capture before they become food for bacteria.

If you host guests regularly or run a small rental, treat the pool like a semi-public facility: test chemicals daily and vacuum at least three times a week. For a private villa used by one or two people, every other day is usually enough in dry season.

sections.h2: A Realistic Weekly Schedule for Sanur
paragraphs: Here is a routine that works well for most Sanur villas:
bullets: Daily (5 min): skim leaves and insects off the surface; confirm the pump is running and water level sits just below the skimmer lip.
Every 2–3 days: brush walls and steps, vacuum the floor, then test free chlorine (aim 1–3 ppm) and pH (7.2–7.6).
Weekly: backwash or clean the cartridge filter; clear the skimmer basket and strainer plate.
Monthly: deep-clean the tile line, inspect return jets for limescale, top up water if it has dropped.
After heavy rain: re-test chemistry within 24 hours—dilution from runoff can drop pH and shock levels quickly.

sections.h2: Where You Can Save Without Cutting Corners
paragraphs: You do not need a full professional service every single day. Skimming, brushing, and basic chemical testing are straightforward tasks you can handle with a net, a long-handled brush, and a test kit. That saves you the cost of a daily visit.

What is worth paying for: a quarterly drain-and-refill once the water has sat for many months, filter media replacement when backwashing no longer restores flow, and any job involving the pump motor, plumbing, or electrical connections near the water. If you ever smell gas near the equipment shed, see sparks at a junction box, or are tempted to mix chlorine with another product—stop and call a licensed technician. Those are not DIY moments.
If budget is tight, send photos via WhatsApp before committing to anything. Prices vary with villa size, access, and how neglected the system is, so a photo-based estimate keeps things transparent.

faq.q: Can I just shock the pool once a month instead of cleaning regularly?
faq.a: Shocking kills existing algae but does not remove the organic matter that caused it. Skip regular skimming and vacuuming, and debris settles into the filter and tile grout, making each subsequent shock less effective. Think of shocking as a reset button, not a substitute for maintenance.

faq.q: Does rainwater from Bali's rainy season really mess up my pool chemistry?
faq.a: Yes. Stormwater running off your roof and garden carries tannins, leaf acids, and sediment. It dilutes chlorine and can drop pH below 7 in a single heavy downpour. After any rain lasting more than an hour, re-test within a day and adjust before the next swim.

faq.q: My pool turned green overnight. What do I do first?
faq.a: Do not add more chlorine blindly—overdosing on top of unbalanced water can make it cloudy for weeks. Skim out every visible leaf or husk, then test free chlorine, combined chlorine, and pH. If combined chlorine is above 0.5 ppm or pH is outside 7.2–7.6, correct those first, then apply a measured shock dose. If the green persists after two days, send a photo to a technician for a targeted plan.

cta: If you are unsure whether your pool needs a deep clean or just a chemical tweak, snap a couple of photos (surface, tile line, filter area) and send them over WhatsApp for a quick assessment.
